To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) house price capitalization is an important economic phenomenon that (ii) is more prevalent in locations with strict land use regulation and/or geographical/ physical supply constraints, (iii) can induce the provision of certain local public goods and (iv) can have adverse implications for a wide range, including intergovernmental aid and the mortgage interest deduction.

(i) the capitalization effect is stronger in areas where there are regulatory and geographical constraints on the supply of housing; (ii) in areas where there is a capitalization effect, local public goods are provided in a more efficient manner than in the absence of such an effect; and (iii), the capitalization effect can be an important source of inefficiency in the allocation of intergovernmental aid.

house price capitalization is a pervasive feature of the real estate market and that it is likely to induce the provision of local public goods, which may have positive or negative effects, depending on the circumstances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which local house prices reflect local public and tax policy.
the extent to which house price capitalization is pervasive, and if so, what the economic implications are of such capitalization effects.
how the capitalization of local public service and fiscal conditions into house prices can influence the provision of public goods and the effectiveness of public policies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
house price capitalization is a complex phenomenon with both desirable and undesirable effects.
house price capitalization is a double-edged sword that may lead to a more efficient provision of local public goods and services but also to a less efficient allocation of resources across space.
the extent to which house prices adjust to public service changes and the broader economic consequences of such adjustment are still largely unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
house price capitalization is an important mechanism that can induce local governments to invest in local public goods and services.
the capitalization of house prices to public services and tax levels is an important phenomenon, but one that is not well understood.

house price capitalization is not only a tool for testing the efficiency of local public services but also a potentially important mechanism for allocating public and private capital across locations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
house price capitalization can have significant economic consequences.
house price capitalization is a powerful mechanism through which local public service and fiscal decisions are transmitted to the private sector and, hence, to the national economy.
the extent of capitalization is not exogenously given.
